Mara drew maps, though what she loved were the blank spaces between them. Every dawn, she unlocked her studio above a bakery and spread yesterday’s surveys across her table. Coastlines, vanished footpaths, doors that opened only in summer: all were useful to someone. She inked them, never labeling places that no longer existed. Her employer preferred tidy maps, with no rumors, no legends, and certainly no handwritten notes. Yet those notes kept appearing, tucked into atlas margins, requesting things like “please remember the lilac tree” or “turn left before the rain.” Mara suspected the city itself was writing to her.

One note arrived in March, folded into the shape of a paper boat. Its ink smelled of apples. Across the river, where warehouses stood on the plans, it showed a courtyard filled with fruit trees. A silver gate divided the entrance from an alley behind the clock factory. At the bottom, beneath a sketch of six silver bells, the message read: “An unplanted seed. Before the first bell. At the hour that has no clock.” Mara examined the lot through her telescope. Soil covered everything, but a chimney rose like a finger, insisting the place had not always been bare.

The clock factory’s roof held a garden where no gardener had climbed in forty years. Mara found the gate waiting beside a ladder. Beyond it, footprints curved through the air, crossing chimneys and sliding over rooftops toward a bell tower with no doors. She followed. Below, trams rang their bells; above, laundry floated in motionless clouds. At a footprint, a sparrow perched on a ledge and chirped a phrase she understood. “First bell,” it said. “Bring something the city has misplaced.” Then it flew toward the river, and Mara discovered a tramcar waiting, its destination board glowing with tomorrow’s date.

The tram carried her past bakeries opening for morning and fishmongers arguing with the sun. When Mara asked what the city had misplaced, the conductor shrugged. “Small things. Spare chances. The moment before someone remembers a name.” At the stop, she boarded carrying a thimble of rainwater from her studio roof. In her pocket lay a pencil stub from the first map she had ever drawn: a crooked house with a star on its chimney. Her mother had called it ugly. Years later, it became the only landmark she recognized in all the shifting streets around her, even by daylight.

The bell tower stood beyond the tram tracks, where a janitor swept leaves from a staircase. He examined Mara’s offerings. “Rain remembers the sky,” he said. “And this remembers your mother.” He tapped the pencil stub, and it drew across the floor, leading upward. “The city collects moments when it changes its mind. Your garden waited for your seed long ago, but no one delivered it. Tonight, the tower will ring for every delay, every apology, every door open. Find the hour without a clock, and the courtyard will remember to bloom.” Orin handed her an acorn of bright silver.

Mara climbed while the city below fell silent, leaving only the staircase’s gentle creaking. The staircase curled through a chamber of clocks, each mechanism labeling a different minute of the night. Some ticked backward. Others leaned together, whispering. One had no face at all. Mara placed her palm against it, and the thimble of rainwater trembled. The pencil drew a door on the wall, while rainwater revealed hinges no one could see. Beyond it waited a nursery lit by moons too numerous to count. Seedlings rested in silver drawers, each tagged with a place that had nearly forgotten growing things.

An attendant in a coat of moss chose a drawer marked “Bellweather Courtyard, possible.” Inside lay one brown seed and a note in Mara’s handwriting. It said, “You will arrive too late. You always draw the safe route.” Her stomach tightened. She remembered an argument with her mother about wasted time, the terrible things neither of them had said, the years spent apologizing for anger instead of offering kindness. The seed felt heavier with every memory. The attendant offered another drawer. “A safer garden,” he said. “One that needs no risk.” Mara chose the seed, and the first bell rang.

The second bell sounded as Mara ran down a stairway that unfolded like paper. The third echoed behind her, then the fourth, each closer than the last. She burst through the clock factory gate just as the first rays of sun struck the river. There was no time for elegance. Kneeling on the empty lot, she pressed the seed into a pocket of soil, poured her rainwater over it, and covered it with both hands. The acorn began to warm. Then a crack split its shell, and an apple tree rose in an impossible breath, scattering leaves across the warehouses.

The fifth bell rang inside the apple tree. Its branches bent toward Mara, and one apple split open, becoming a ring of tiny candles. Candlelight spilled across the courtyard, illuminating paths, benches, and a hundred other trees that seemed to be waiting underground. People emerged from the factory doors, blinking. Children laughed. Someone began playing a violin badly and beautifully. When the sixth bell sounded, the river turned the color of dawn, and Mara understood that the hour without a clock was not hidden at all. It was the moment a city decided what to remember together in its streets.

At noon, Orin found Mara beneath the leaves, sketching the courtyard for her employer. He carried a paper boat filled with apple blossoms and a brass bell for her studio door. “No need for maps now?” he asked. She looked at the paths crowded with strangers sharing fruit, at the chimney still visible above the branches, at the lot that now held a small piece of impossible morning. “Especially maps now,” she said. The city had not repaired its mistakes, but it had made room for one. Mara drew the gate, leaving a white gap where somebody might someday enter.
